title: Running it
summary: One repository runs in three shapes, all on Docker Compose. Developers build the local stack from source. A release runs digest-pinned images on one host, and an overlay moves the database to a second host. None of the shapes is highly available.

boxes.label: Simulators
boxes.detail: Scripts that publish Sparkplug B or vendor payloads through the real broker, so the whole pipeline runs without hardware. A passing simulator run is not hardware verification.

boxes.label: Single-node release
boxes.detail: Everything on one host: Caddy, the API as php-fpm behind nginx, portal, admin, five workers and the scheduler, the runtime, TimescaleDB, NATS, Mosquitto with broker-admin, and the monitoring stack. Application images come from the manifest by digest and state lives in one directory on the host. It is recoverable from a checkpoint, not highly available.

boxes.label: Browsers and devices
boxes.detail: Caddy publishes 80 and 443 and the broker publishes 8883. The host playbook opens exactly those three ports and allows SSH only on the VPN interface.

boxes.label: Two-server shape
boxes.detail: When DATABASE_HOST is not the bundled service, manage.py adds an overlay that leaves the local TimescaleDB out and gives it a database client container for psql and pg_dump. The address must be a private IPv4 address routed through the WireGuard tunnel, or validation fails. Restore refuses this shape: a checkpoint is restored on an isolated single node first.

boxes.label: Database host
boxes.detail: The second server runs its own small Compose file: TimescaleDB listening only on its private tunnel address, with the same rendered role script as the app host, and a node exporter that the app host's Prometheus scrapes with a database role label.

steps.text: Every shape starts from the same repository: apps, services, shared packages and contracts. Open it to see what depends on what.
Locally, Compose builds each service from source with no bind mounts, so you rebuild a service to see a change.
Simulators stand in for devices and publish through the local broker over TLS, the same path hardware takes.
A v* tag runs the release workflow: checks, eight images pushed by digest, and a manifest that names them.
On the host, manage.py deploys exactly the images in the manifest. Open Release to follow the steps.
Only Caddy (80, 443) and the broker (8883) face the internet. Everything else stays on the private Compose network.
Setting DATABASE_HOST to a private address turns the same release into the two-server shape; nothing else changes.
The API, workers and runtime then reach TimescaleDB on the second host through the tunnel. If the address is public or not routed through it, the deploy is refused.
